title: Embodied learning using a tangible user interface: The effects of haptic perception and selective pointing on a spatial learning task

findings.antecedent: Experimental group (Mouse Permanent Display, Mouse Selective Pointing, TUI Permanent Display, TUI Selective Pointing)
findings.quote: Participants in the four experimental groups did not differ regarding their performance in the prior knowledge test as tested using an ANOVA, F(3, 92) = .2014, p = .895.

findings.antecedent: Experimental group (Mouse Permanent Display, Mouse Selective Pointing, TUI Permanent Display, TUI Selective Pointing)
findings.quote: A Kruskall-Wallis test for the question item regarding if and when the participants had learned heart anatomy revealed no significant difference between the four groups with a chi-square test, either [x² (3, N = 96) = 2.19, p = .535].

findings.antecedent: Experimental group (Mouse Permanent Display, Mouse Selective Pointing, TUI Permanent Display, TUI Selective Pointing)
findings.quote: Regarding spatial abilities, there was neither a difference in spatial ability between the groups as revealed through an ANOVA [F(3,92) = .43, p = .729]
nor a difference between genders as assessed using a t-test [t(53.76) = 1.28, p = .207].

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse)
findings.mechanism: Holding and touching a complex three-dimensional object facilitates the formation of a coherent spatial representation, providing a persistent guide for orientation, and integrating visual and verbal information.
findings.quote: Retention performance was higher when the TUI was used instead of the mouse

findings.antecedent: Interaction between input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.mechanism: The effect of the label display mode is different for the two input devices: Selective pointing is better with mouse, while permanent display is better with TUI.
findings.quote: a significant interaction between input device and label display mode [F(1, 92) = 6.78, p = .011, η = .06]

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.mechanism: Transfer test may have been too difficult for participants without prior medical training, or TUI does not affect performance in cognitively challenging tasks.
findings.quote: the transfer task (composite score of the three test sheets with a maximum of 22 correct items) yielded no significant differences in a 2 × 2 ANOVA (input device × label display mode), all ps ≥ .555

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.quote: While we found no significant effect regarding intrinsic load (all ps ≥ .129)

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse)
findings.mechanism: Additional haptic input from TUI acts as landmarks, providing a stable reference frame and using multiple sensory modalities, thereby lowering cognitive load.
findings.quote: Using the TUI resulted in a lower germane load (indicating less difficulty with the learning task) with a significant main effect of input device, F(1, 92) = 8.08, p = .006, η = .08.

findings.antecedent: Interaction between input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.mechanism: Permanent display mode increases cognitive load when using the mouse, but lowers cognitive load when using the tangible and pen.
findings.quote: there were significant interactions between input device and label display mode... F(1, 92) = 4.11, p = .046, η = .04

findings.antecedent: Interaction between input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.mechanism: Permanent display mode increases cognitive load when using the mouse, but lowers cognitive load when using the tangible and pen.

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse)
findings.mechanism: The dynamic and natural experience of manipulating a virtual 3D object with a tangible physical object.
findings.quote: There was a main effect of the factor input device on interest [F(1, 91 ) = 6, p = .016, η = .06], indicating that the TUI led to an increased interest in the learning task.

findings.antecedent: Interaction between input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.mechanism: Selective pointing promoted a feeling of efficacy for mouse users, while this feature was detrimental for efficacy in the TUI condition due to motor coordination.
findings.quote: In regard to efficacy, we found an interaction between input device and label display mode, F(1, 92) = 4.17, p = .044, η = .04.

findings.antecedent: Input device (Tangible User Interface vs Mouse) and label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.quote: No effect was found on the scale challenge (all ps ≥ .54).

findings.antecedent: Label display mode (Permanent vs Selective Pointing)
findings.mechanism: Preference for the selective pointing mode, possibly due to perceived interactivity and engagement.
findings.quote: There was a main effect of selective pointing on the scale “hedonic quality – stimulation” [F(1, 91) = 7.78, p = .006, η = .08], indicating a preference for the selective pointing mode

findings.mechanism: TUI offers a multi-sensory user experience which is perceived as better suited for this particular learning task.
findings.quote: as well as a main effect of input device on “pragmatic quality” [F(1, 92) = 7.72, p = .007, η = .08] in favor of the TUI.

stimuli.description: Custom-built learning environment featuring a 3D model of a human heart with 21 floating labels. Interaction via a regular computer mouse or a tangible user interface (TUI) consisting of a motion-tracked plastic heart model (200g) with a stylus pen. Label display modes were permanent (all labels visible) or selective pointing (labels appear on click/touch).

limitations: Position of the virtual heart could not be changed in mouse conditions due to technical reasons, which was overwhelming for most participants.
The transfer test may have been too difficult for participants without prior medical training.
The TUI did not affect performance in a cognitively challenging task such as labeling cross-sections.
Too many factors (spatial ability, learning strategies, short learning time) might exert higher influence on cognitively challenging tasks.
Longer learning times or repeated presentations are needed to assess whether deeper processing is facilitated by embodied interaction design featuring haptic perception.
Future research should assess the influence of different learning styles when learning with multimodal user interfaces.
Design recommendations for TUIs are limited to similar learning tasks and relatively complex objects small enough to be held with one hand.
Less complex or unhandy objects may be equally well or better learned using a traditional mouse interface.
The two-handed use of TUIs had a detrimental effect on learning in the selective pointing condition.
Learning tests should have made use of the motor representations acquired while pointing at the model with the stylus pen to potentially show advantage for TUI selective pointing.
Future studies should investigate whether single-handed 3D pointing devices offer comparably positive effects as the mouse pointing condition.
More factors influence the usefulness of the selective pointing feature, such as learning time frame and the amount of elements to be learned.
More research is needed to disentangle the roles of visual load, motor load, and processing load when using self-cueing techniques such as selective pointing.
More research is required to validate and formalize the cost-benefit model of Embodied Cognition.
The role of motor information in learning tasks should be systematically investigated further.
Additional research on Embodied Cognitive Load Theory is required to confirm results and to further clarify the role of multisensory perception, interactivity, and meta-cognition.
